## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11 (PTS Vin IV 34) formulates the monastic rule prohibiting the intentional destruction of plant life (*bhūtagāmapātavyatāya pācittiyam*), stipulating that a monk who damages vegetation commits an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiya*) [Bechert 1992; Schmithausen 2009]. In the canonical word analysis (*padabhājanīya*), *bhūtagāma* ("vegetative growth") is defined via five modes of propagation (*pañca bījajātāni*): plants generated from roots (*mūlabīja*), stems (*khandhabīja*), joints (*phalubīja*), cuttings (*aggabīja*), and seeds (*bījabīja*) [Clarke, Pārājika]. The archaic term *pātavyatā* has been analyzed by scholars as denoting uncontrolled or ruthless behavior toward plants [Schmithausen 2009]. In the origin narrative, the rule is motivated by public reproach: householders complained that cutting trees harmed living beings endowed with one sense-faculty (*ekindriyaṁ jīva*) or destroyed the abodes of tree deities (*devatā*) [Deutsch and Bontekoe 1999; Bechert 1992; Schmithausen 1991; Schmithausen 2009]. In later ethical and legal analysis, destroying vegetation—such as plucking flowers with devotion to honor the Triple Gem—is classified as an infraction of institutional monastic convention (*paṇṇattivajja*) rather than an intrinsically unwholesome act (*lokavajja*) [Entrance to the Vinaya 1969; Keown 1992].

 Whereas the Pali Pātimokkha rule refers strictly to plants (*bhūtagāma*), many parallels across other schools and standard Suttapiṭaka formulas (such as the *Dīgha Nikāya* stock description *bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambha*) explicitly prohibit injuring both seeds and plants [Buddhism into the Year 2000; Bechert 1992; Schmithausen 2009]. The Pali and Dharmaguptaka traditions uniquely place this rule immediately after the prohibition against digging soil (Pācittiya 10), reflecting a shared thematic cluster [Schmithausen 1991]. Text-reuse computation in DharmaNexus automatically aligns segments of the text with the Tibetan Bhikṣuṇīvinayavibhaṅga (D0005) and Vinayakārikā (D4123), as well as Sanskrit Prātimokṣasūtra fragments [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records 356 matching passages across 84 texts, sharing extensive phrasing with neighboring Vibhaṅga rules (especially Pācittiya 10, 13, and 20), Khandhaka sections (Kd 1, Kd 6, Kd 15), and commentaries including the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā and Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā [DharmaNexus].
